[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
'''Daniel Glasco''' was associated with Lower Norfolk County in the Colony of Virginia during the late seventeenth century. His date and place of birth have not been identified.

The spelling '''Glasco''' is used in the published abstract of the only contemporary record presently identified for him. The original record should be inspected before concluding that this was his consistent surname spelling.

May be a grandson of [[Glasgow-1157|Robert Glasgow II (abt.1612-abt.1690)]]

=== Marriage to Mary Gamon ===

Daniel married '''Mary Gamon''', also rendered Gammon in later accounts, before 4 October 1693.

The will of Mary's father, '''John Gamon''', was dated 4 October 1693 and proved on 15 March 1694. Its published abstract identifies Daniel Glasco as John Gamon's son-in-law and Mary as Daniel's wife. John left Daniel and Mary eighty acres of land bordering Richford Swamp.<ref name="GamonWill">Charles Fleming McIntosh, ''Brief Abstract of Lower Norfolk County and Norfolk County Wills, 1637–1710'' (Virginia: Colonial Dames of America in the State of Virginia, 1914), p. 149, abstract of the will of John Gamon, dated 4 October 1693 and proved 15 March 1694; cited and discussed in Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf ''Research Report''] (1 March 2016), p. 3.</ref>

The record directly establishes that:

* Daniel and Mary were married by 4 October 1693;
* Mary's father was John Gamon; and
* Daniel and Mary received land bordering Richford Swamp.

Richford Swamp was situated in Elizabeth River Parish, Lower Norfolk County.<ref name="LegacyReport">Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf ''Research Report''] (1 March 2016), pp. 3–4.</ref>

The will abstract does not identify Daniel's parents, birthplace, age, occupation or children.

Daniel was alive on 4 October 1693. His date and place of death have not been identified.

== Research Notes ==
=== Title-clause reinspection, 20 October 2026 ===
The enlarged original of Daniel Glasco’s 1729 deed describes the land as now in Daniel’s tenure and occupation. It does not name William as a predecessor or identify a father. The earlier possible William reading is withdrawn. Mary is explicitly Daniel’s wife, and the tract is part of Henry Slade’s 330-acre patent. This remains a compatible comparison for [[Glasgow-3322|Daniel Glasgow]], Mary Gamon’s husband in 1693, rather than a proved lifetime identity. The title chain from the Gamon property is still missing. [[Glasgow-1158|Daniel Glasgow]] remains [[Glasgow-428|William Glasgow]]’s possible working father at 42%; this inspection supplies no additional paternity evidence.<ref name="DanielDeedTitle20261020">Princess Anne County, Deeds and Wills Book 4, Part 1 (1724–1735), manuscript p.207, DGS 7645780, image 150; original image reinspected 20 October 2026. https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-99PX-F3DX. Original deed body and acknowledgment reinspected at enlarged resolution on 20 October 2026. The possible William predecessor reading is withdrawn: the title clause describes Daniel’s tenure and occupation. No father is named. Exact execution dating and profile identity remain unresolved; personal acknowledgment, rather than registration alone, establishes survival to 3 September 1729.</ref>

=== Two Daniels in Currituck ===
The 1693 Mary Gamon husband remains this profile’s primary record identity. The two Currituck Daniels of 1718–1719 are compatible comparisons; this profile is not automatically Junior or distinct from Daniel-1158.

The published Currituck tax transcriptions distinguish two contemporary Daniels. The 1718 levy list separately enters Daniell Glasco Ser. and Daniel Glasco Jur., each assessed for one tithable and 15 shillings. The 1719 return repeats the distinction: Senior has one tract of 250 acres and land tax of 6s 3d; Junior’s land columns are blank. Blank columns are not proof that Junior owned no land. The 1715 land-tax return separately records Daniell Glasco paying 6s 6d on one 260-acre tract on 27 March.

These are newly reviewed published transcriptions attributed to NCSA Colonial Court Records, Taxes & Accounts, CCR 190; manuscript images were not inspected. Senior and Junior distinguish the two entries and suggest relative age, but do not state father and son. The two years support retaining at least two record-defined Daniels, without supplying their exact ages, wives, children or a physical household arrangement. The similar 1715 and 1719 acreages are a possible continuity clue, not proof of the same tract or man.

The existing profiles Daniel [[Glasgow-1158]] and Daniel [[Glasgow-3322]] are compatible comparison accounts, not automatic matches to Senior and Junior respectively. Both are attached to Robert-1157 in the current tree and may themselves duplicate one adult; the fact that the returns contain two Daniels does not prove that these two profiles represent those two men. Daniel-3322’s account represents the Mary Gamon husband named in 1693. The 1729 Norfolk Daniel/Mary deed is a further compatible identity, not a proved continuation into either Currituck taxpayer. Daniel-1158’s inherited 1712 death remains unverified: it cannot establish which later Daniel is excluded, nor should a later same-name entry automatically extend his life. Preserve both profiles and their vital fields while testing these identities.

Retain Daniel [[Glasgow-1158]] as William [[Glasgow-428]]’s possible working father at 42% subjective confidence. The established early Daniel name in the Norfolk–Currituck region, the 1693 Daniel/Mary Gamon household and the later Currituck Daniel tax entries provide a plausible older local family for William’s 1738 and 1746 household. William’s inherited circa-1685 birth is an estimate, not a recorded age. The existing older Daniel account is a useful provisional choice, but the evidence does not identify the taxpayer as that profile or name William as his son. The two contemporary Daniels make the adult identification materially less specific than a single-name reconstruction suggests.

42% is the first individual assessment of this existing father placement, not an increase from a previous numerical probability or a newly discovered father. A younger local Daniel, another Glasgow father, or a collateral relationship remains possible; the two modern Daniel accounts could also duplicate the same man. William’s 1746 will names his children and an unnamed grandfather of Sarah, but does not identify that grandfather as paternal or as Daniel. No mother, Scottish origin, Robert ancestry, father replacement, merge or vital-date change is selected. The tax suffixes alone are not a basis for connecting the two Daniels as father and son.

Trace the 260/250-acre Currituck property separately from the 80 acres at Richford Swamp in the 1693 Gamon will and the 100-acre 1729 Norfolk/Princess Anne conveyance. An acreage resemblance is not a title chain. Compare deeds, cattle marks and associated people for the two Daniels before allocating either taxpayer to a modern profile or treating the unnamed grandfather in William’s will as Daniel.<ref name="CurrituckTaxReview">[https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/tax/1715land.html Stuart Chaplain, NCGenWeb transcription of Currituck 1715 land taxes, 27 March entry; North Carolina State Archives, Colonial Court Records, Taxes & Accounts, CCR 190]; [https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/tax/1718levies.html Stuart Chaplain, NCGenWeb transcription of Currituck 1718 levies, third displayed section; NCSA Colonial Court Records, Taxes & Accounts, CCR 190]; [https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/tax/1719levies.html Stuart Chaplain, NCGenWeb transcription of Currituck 1719 levies and land tax, first displayed section; NCSA Colonial Court Records, Taxes & Accounts, CCR 190]. Tax transcriptions checked 18 October 2026; manuscripts not inspected. Earlier context reused: Charles F. McIntosh, Brief Abstract of Lower Norfolk County and Norfolk County Wills1637–1710 (1914), p.149, John Gamon will4 October1693, proved15 March1694, independently inspected30 September2026 and cited in [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf LegacyTree2016 report p.3]; [https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/wills/glasgowwilliam1746.html William Glasgow will30 September1746, proved7 April1747, previously reviewed transcription].</ref>


=== Birth date ===

Daniel has previously been assigned a birth year of 1613.

The cited source for that date is an International Genealogical Index entry submitted by an unidentified contributor. The entry contains no supporting source information.<ref name="IGI">The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, “International Genealogical Index (IGI),” database, ''FamilySearch'', [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/2:1:MDL3-HTF entry for Daniel Glasgow] (accessed 4 April 2025); submitted by user jence5408, with no source information supplied.</ref>

A submitted IGI entry records a contributor's assertion. Without an underlying baptism, Bible, will, deed or other historical record, it does not establish that Daniel was born in 1613.

Daniel's birth date and birthplace should therefore be left unknown.

For database purposes, the only certain statement is that he was born before 4 October 1693, when he was recorded as Mary's husband.

=== Unsupported Scottish parentage ===

'''[[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Ivey-2264|Deborah Ivey]]''' have previously been attached as Daniel's parents.

No inspected record identifies either person as his father or mother.

The will of John Gamon identifies Daniel's wife and father-in-law but does not name Daniel's parents. No Scottish baptism, marriage, testament, land record or migration record has been found connecting Daniel with Robert Glasgow or Deborah Ivey.

Both parental relationships should be removed.

Daniel should also not be attached as a child of '''[[Glasgow-3938|Robert Glasgow]]''', the cordiner who married Jonet or Janet Thomsone in Edinburgh in 1652. No evidence connects that Edinburgh household with Daniel or colonial Virginia.

=== Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson tradition ===

Many online family trees instead identify Daniel as a son of a Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson or Johnston.

A professional review of the family found that this relationship was repeated in online trees but that those trees supplied no documentary evidence supporting it.<ref name="LegacyReport" />

No contemporary record presently establishes that:

* Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson were Daniel's parents;
* Daniel was born in Scotland;
* Daniel migrated from Scotland to Virginia; or
* Daniel belonged to the Scottish Glasgow families represented by the earlier profiles.

Any attachment to Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson should remain uncertain or be removed until a contemporary parentage record is found.

=== Possible connection with Robert Glascocke ===

A Robert Glascocke was documented in the Elizabeth River area before Daniel's known appearance there.

Robert Glascocke received:

* a patent for 200 acres in Elizabeth City County on 7 October 1635; and
* a patent for another fifty acres in Lower New Norfolk County on 10 June 1639.

A 1640 court order also referred to religious services being held at Robert Glascocke's house while a meetinghouse was being built.<ref name="LegacyReport" />

The shared locality and broadly similar surnames make Robert Glascocke a person worth investigating as a possible relative.

They do not prove that:

* Robert Glascocke was Daniel's father;
* Glascocke and Glasco were forms used by the same family;
* Robert married Ann Johnson;
* Daniel inherited Robert's land; or
* either man belonged to a Scottish Glasgow family.

Robert Glascocke should not be attached as Daniel's father without a deed, will, court record or other document connecting them.

=== Surname ===

The published abstract of John Gamon's will records Daniel's surname as '''Glasco'''.

Later records and compiled genealogies use variants including:

* Glasco;
* Glasgow;
* Glascock;
* Glasscock; and
* Glascocke.

Surname spelling was not fully standardised during this period, but similarity alone does not prove that all these records concern one family.

The original will should be inspected to establish the spelling used by the clerk. Until then, Glasco is the best-supported spelling for Daniel himself, with Glasgow retained as an alternate form where appropriate.

=== Children ===

No inspected contemporary record identifies a child of Daniel Glasco and Mary Gamon.

Later family trees attribute children and extensive descendants to the couple, but those relationships should not be treated as established solely because they appear in compiled genealogies.

Each proposed child requires separate evidence, such as:

* a baptism or parish entry;
* a deed describing the relationship;
* a will naming the child;
* a guardianship record;
* an apprenticeship record;
* a court order; or
* a documented chain of inherited land.

Any existing child attachments should remain uncertain pending review of their individual evidence.

=== The inherited property ===

John Gamon's will left Daniel and Mary eighty acres bordering Richford Swamp.

Tracing that property may be the best route for identifying Daniel's later life and possible children. Deeds involving its later sale, inheritance or division may name Daniel's heirs or establish whether he had died.

The original will, probate proceedings and subsequent land records should be obtained rather than relying solely on the published abstract.

=== Death ===

Daniel's date and place of death are unknown.

He was alive when John Gamon's will was written on 4 October 1693. The will's probate on 15 March 1694 does not necessarily prove Daniel was still living on that later date.

His death should therefore be recorded as after 4 October 1693 only if an estimated date is required. No precise death place should be assigned.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining records include:

* the original will of John Gamon;
* the complete probate file and estate accounts;
* deeds concerning the eighty acres bordering Richford Swamp;
* Lower Norfolk County court orders;
* Elizabeth River Parish records;
* later Norfolk and Princess Anne County deeds and probate records;
* records identifying Daniel and Mary's children or heirs;
* land records concerning Robert Glascocke's patents;
* evidence establishing whether Glasco, Glasgow and Glascocke were used for the same family;
* contemporary records concerning Ann Johnson or Johnston;
* any immigration or transportation record for Daniel;
* a will or estate administration for Daniel;
* a will or estate administration for Mary; and
* the original evidence underlying the submitted IGI entry.

A possible identification concerns Daniel Glasco. Daniel Glasco, Norfolk planter, conveyed 100 acres to Richard Linton with the consent of Mary, explicitly his wife. The court endorsement says Daniel personally acknowledged the deed on 3 September 1729, establishing survival to that date.<ref>Princess Anne County, Deeds and Wills Book4 Part1 (1724–1735), manuscript p.207, DGS7645780; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-99PX-F3DX record].</ref> Inspected original deed endorsement. Registration alone is not used as a life boundary. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Daniel Glasco. Daneill Glasco witnesses Richard Johnson’s Norfolk will dated 26 February 1729/30, with Richard Linton and John Moy. The will was proved on 18 September 1730.<ref>McIntosh, Norfolk County will abstracts, printed p. 122 (PDF image p. 122), Richard Johnson will; [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/166084/ record].</ref> Printed will abstract inspected, not the original will manuscript. No father or survival-to-probate inference. [[Glasgow-428|William Glasgow]] is an associated research case and is not named in this entry. The identification remains uncertain.

== Acknowledgements ==

This profile was previously attached to an unsupported Scottish family and carried an unsourced birth year of 1613. It has been revised to represent Daniel Glasco, husband of Mary Gamon, documented through the 1693–1694 will of John Gamon.
